# Ledger scale bench

Generated by `scripts/bench-ledger.ts` (`npx tsx scripts/bench-ledger.ts --sizes 10000` and `--sizes 100000`,
one size at a time, each in its own temp project under the container's own `/tmp`, deleted after) inside the
Node 22 clean-room container (`sidewise-test:node22`, `docker run --rm --memory 1500m -v $PWD:/app -w /app
--user root sidewise-test:node22 ...`, host repo bind-mounted, container's own filesystem for the generated
ledgers) — **Node v22.23.3**, confirmed via the bench's own printed `node=` line, so `node:sqlite` is real, not
the fallback. Host machine: a shared box (the same class of machine earlier docs in this repo ran on, under
similar load-sensitivity caveats — p50 is the number this doc trusts, p95 is reported honestly but noisier).
**Sizes are 10,000 and 100,000 runs only, both real, both measured — 1,000,000 is a labelled extrapolation
only (see below), never claimed as measured.**

This is **fix round 1** of Task 29 (revised), after a profiling review measured exactly why the first cut
(commit `95c5aa1`) was slow: `PRAGMA quick_check` ran on every open (~99% of a point call's own time at 100k), a
reuse MISS walked every candidate run for the provider even when a single missing `answer_keys` row already
proved no run ever held the key, `appendLine` read the whole log just to check its last byte, `appendOutcome`
did a full ledger scan for a check the index can now answer, and read-only callers (view, findRun) could end up
rebuilding the on-disk index under the SAME lock a real writer needed. This run measures the fixed code (`HEAD`
after those fixes) with the **same generator and same sizes as the original run**, so the two are a fair
before/after, row for row.

**Index strategy — not yet designed, backlog:** this round fixed measured hot spots (skip quick_check unless
there's real suspicion, a missing-row shortcut for reuse misses, targeted byte reads instead of full-file
reads, an index-backed outcome lookup, and lock-safe self-healing for read-only callers). It did **not** touch
the schema, the rebuild pragmas, or the db/log size ratio — those are explicitly out of scope for this round
(the owner's own call: the index strategy itself will be designed later). The db/log ratio and `rebuild`'s own
cost below are carried over unchanged from the original run and are not re-analyzed here.

## Bottom line

**Every equivalence and self-heal test passes against the real engine, in this same container, including four
new tests this round added** (a stale schema_version triggers a rebuild; a real multi-hop `reusedFrom` chain and
a blocked-newest-holder both resolve correctly; a query that throws mid-`fn` falls back with identical results
and no leaked partial state; the `node:sqlite` warning filter is suppressed end-to-end while an unrelated
warning still prints) — the binding invariant (deleting or corrupting `index.db` never changes an answer, only
speed) holds throughout. On top of that, this round's fixes **clear the < 100 ms per-call target at 100k by a
wide margin** for every op on the paid-call path: `reuseHit`, `reuseMiss`, `exactReuseMiss`, `findRunById` and
`appendOutcome` all land **under 1.3 ms p95** at 100k (previously 93 ms–3.0 s), and the real end-to-end paid
`class` call is **32.6 ms** at 100k (previously 799 ms). `rebuild` is still slow (15.6 s p50 at 100k) — expected,
since rebuild pragmas were explicitly not tuned this round — and the db/log ratio is unchanged (1.158 at 10k,
0.410 at 100k, carried over from the original run, not re-measured).

## What changed, and why (fix round 1)

- **`PRAGMA quick_check` only on suspicion, not on every open.** A near-free header-only check
  (`page_count * page_size` vs the file's actual size) catches the truncation/crash-mid-write case quick_check
  also catches, at a fraction of the cost; quick_check itself now only runs when that cheap check fails.
  Consumers already re-verify what they read from the ledger (readRecordAt's own bounds/parse checks, findRun's
  own re-match, view's own re-check against the real record), so a bad page this cheap check can't see still
  costs a rebuild the next time something notices — never a wrong answer.
- **A missing-row shortcut for reuse misses.** `answer_keys` is checked directly for existence before any
  candidate walk: if no run ever held a key, no walk could ever find it either (the linear oracle would also
  find nothing), so `lookupAnswers`/`exactReuse` skip the O(candidates) walk entirely for that key. This is the
  single largest win this round — a genuine "new question" reuse miss at 100k dropped from 2.3 s to under 1 ms.
- **`appendLine` reads one byte, not the whole log**, to decide whether it needs to insert a line break before
  appending — a targeted `openSync`/`readSync` at `size - 1`, matching the discipline `checkTail` already used.
- **`appendOutcome`'s "already recorded?" check reads the index's own outcomes table** (now carrying `uid` too,
  schema version bumped to 2) instead of a full `readLedger` scan.
- **Read-only callers never rebuild or catch up the on-disk index under the writers' lock.** `findRun`,
  `exactReuse`, and a sweep verb's `--dry-run` planning are always `readOnly`: when the on-disk index isn't
  already fresh, they fall back to the in-memory linear scan (always correct, just not persisted) instead of
  taking the lock — a real writer's own `withLock` call (5 s timeout) can no longer be made to fail by a casual
  read that happened to trigger a 100k rebuild. `view` (place mode) is the same. A non-read-only caller
  (`checkLedger`, `nextRunNumber`, a real append) still self-heals on disk as before, and now re-checks
  freshness after acquiring the lock rather than blindly repeating whatever a racing process already fixed.
  `rebuildToDisk` also renames the new file over the old one directly (relying on `renameSync`'s atomic
  replace) instead of deleting the old file first, closing the "briefly missing" window a concurrent opener
  could otherwise observe.
- **`node:sqlite` is resolved lazily and synchronously (`process.getBuiltinModule`), on first real use, not at
  module import time.** The previous top-level `await import('node:sqlite')` ran (and installed the warning
  filter) the instant `ledger/index.ts` was first imported by ANYTHING — including a library consumer who never
  touches the ledger, since this module is reachable from the package's own public export. `runSqlite`'s
  catch-all now also re-throws a genuine `LedgerError` (corrupt ledger content) instead of swallowing it into a
  fallback retry that would only rediscover the same corruption a second time.
- **Four tests this round added**, closing gaps a profiling review flagged: a stale `schema_version` triggers a
  rebuild; a hand-built ledger with a REAL multi-hop `reusedFrom` chain and a blocked-newest-holder pair proves
  both trace correctly (the existing randomized test's generator never populates `reusedFrom` at all, so this
  was previously untested); a query that throws mid-`fn` (test-only fault injection) falls back to the linear
  scan with identical results and no leaked partial state; the `node:sqlite` `ExperimentalWarning` is suppressed
  end-to-end through a real ledger touch while an unrelated warning still prints, run in the Node 22 container.

## 1,000,000: extrapolated, not measured

Not run this round either — out of scope (10k and 100k only), and, independently, Task 27's own finding still
applies: `toJsonl`-shaped generation runs into Node's `buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH` (≈512 MiB) somewhere
north of ~500,000 records on this build. The per-call numbers this round (all comfortably under 1.3 ms p95 at
100k) have enough headroom that a 1M ledger's point-lookup cost is not expected to be the concern; `rebuild`'s
own cost, not tuned this round, would still scale with the untouched db/log ratio and rebuild path — see the
original run's own extrapolation for that shape, unchanged here.

## Rebuild / maintenance cadence

Unchanged from the original run's own finding: no proactive, size-triggered rebuild is needed (unlike the old
JSON index's `REBUILD_SIZE_RATIO`) — a SQL table's rows grow proportionally with the ledger, and a catch-up only
ever touches the bytes actually added since the last one. The self-heal triggers (missing, unreadable, a
suspicious size that fails quick_check, a schema-version mismatch, a log shorter than `upto`, or a fingerprint
mismatch) are unchanged by this round's fixes — only the COST of checking them, and of what happens once a
reuse miss or an outcome check needs an answer, changed.
